fetched_contents.text: Current evidence on medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty in patients 60 and younger: a narrative review Abstract Background and Objective Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a debilitating condition that significantly impacts mobility and quality of life, particularly in younger, active patients. Medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) is becoming increasingly utilized as a joint-preserving alternative to total knee arthroplasty (TKA) for treating isolated medial compartment OA. This review evaluates current evidence on medial UKA in patients age 60 years or younger, assessing survivability, functional outcomes, and return to activity rates to provide insight into its viability for this patient population. Methods A literature search was conducted using PubMed, MEDLINE, SPORTDiscus identifying studies published from 2015 to 2025 evaluating outcomes of medial UKA. Inclusion criteria encompassed original studies in English that focused on medial UKA for knee OA in patients aged ≤60 years and studies that provided separate age-stratified data for this subgroup. Exclusion criteria included review articles, case reports, studies including concomitant procedures, and those analyzing lateral UKA, patellofemoral joint arthroplasty or patients >60 years of age. A total of 19 studies were selected, and the outcome variables of interest included implant survivability, patient-reported outcomes, range of motion (ROM), and return to activity. Key Content and Findings Medial UKA offers advantages over TKA, such as bone preservation, rapid recovery, and improved knee kinematics. Studies reported survivorship rates exceeding 90% at 10 and 15 years, with improved patient-reported outcomes and ROM. Short-term return-to-activity rates were high, with over 90% of patients resuming physical activity postoperatively. However, concerns regarding longer-term implant durability and performance under high functional demands are still present, particularly in young, athletic individuals engaging in high-impact sports. Conclusions Overall, medial UKA is a promising option for patients age 60 years and younger with isolated medial compartment OA, offering good long-term implant survivability and functional outcomes, relatively low complication rates and high rates of short-term return to activity. Future studies should review longer-term outcomes of medial UKA in patients age 60 years and younger. Keywords: Medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (medial UKA), knee osteoarthritis (knee OA), activity, sports Introduction Background Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a progressive degenerative joint disease significantly affecting quality of life and functional mobility. In the United States, symptomatic knee OA affects over 14 million adults, with a median age of diagnosis at approximately 55 years. Furthermore, 10% of adults 60 years and older will experience symptomatic knee OA (1). Knee OA is associated with substantial economic costs, with annual per-patient expenses ranging from $1,442 to $21,335, a figure steadily increasing (1). Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) remains the gold standard treatment for end-stage OA in older adults, offering implant survivorship exceeding 15 years (2). However, concerns regarding implant durability, activity limitations, and future revisions have led to the exploration of joint-preserving procedures for younger, active patients. Effective management of knee OA requires an understanding of knee anatomy and biomechanics. The knee primarily functions as a hinge joint, composed of the distal femur, tibial plateau, patella, and fibular head. It moves along three primary axes: flexion-extension in the sagittal plane, internal-external rotation of the tibial plateau in the axial plane, and patellar tracking within the trochlear groove (3). Stability is maintained primarily by the anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments (ACL, PCL), and medial and lateral collateral ligaments (MCL, LCL). Patellar alignment is supported by the medial patellofemoral ligaments, patellar tendon, trochlear groove and tibial tubercle. Specifically, the integrity and tensioning of the MCL is important for stability of the medial compartment and durability of implants (4). Coronal plane alignment, defined by a mechanical axis extending from the femoral head to the tibial plafond, significantly influences load distribution within the joint. The natural varus alignment of the knee, results in medialization of the mechanical axis, increasing mechanical stress and accelerating medial compartment cartilage degeneration (5). As a result, isolated medial compartment OA has been reported to be the most prevalent form of knee OA (5). Initial management of isolated medial compartment OA typically involves conservative interventions such as activity modification, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications, physical therapy, corticosteroid injections, and viscosupplementation. While effective for symptom relief, these treatments do not alter disease progression (6,7). For mild to moderate arthritis with focal cartilage defects, cartilage-preserving procedures including microfracture, mesenchymal stem cells, matrix-induced autologous chondrocyte implantation and osteochondral autograft/allograft transplantation are available. Osteochondral allograft (OCA) transplantation, is often considered for patients with osteochondral lesions larger than 2 cm × 2 cm. While often regarded as a salvage procedure, OCA has demonstrated promising results, with Nielsen et al. reporting survivorship rates of 91% and 89% at 5 and 10 years, respectively, with over 75% returning to sport (8,9). Treatment options such as high tibial osteotomy (HTO) and implantable shock absorbers (ISAs) function to alter load distribution for symptomatic relief in young patients with isolated medial compartment OA (10,11). fetched_contents.text: Unicompartmental Knee Arthroplasty: Modes of Failure and Conversion to Total Knee Arthroplasty Abstract Despite the excellent success rates of the modern unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA), results of knee replacement registries still shows a relatively high revision and failure rate for UKA, especially when compared with traditional total knee arthroplasty (TKA). Degeneration of the unreplaced compartments has been reported in both mobile and fixed designs. When the revision is required, most of failed UKAs are converted to TKAs. Surgical challenges of the UKA revision, and outcomes of UKA converted to TKA are still debated in literature. Keywords: unicompartmental knee arthroplasty, polyethylene, loosening, bearing dislocation, revision, conversion Introduction During the last 20 years, the use of unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) has considerably increased. Between 1998 and 2005, use of UKA increased at a rate nearly triple that of total knee arthroplasty (TKA). 1 UKA can be performed through a minimally invasive approach and is associated with a relatively low incidence of complications. 2 3 Several reports have already demonstrated survival rates greater than 90% at 10 years after modern UKA implantation. 1 4 5 6 7 Despite this, results of knee replacement registries still show a relatively high revision and failure rate for UKA, especially when compared with traditional TKA. 8 Failures of UKAs have distinctive characteristics, and consensus on the causes and the proper treatment methods has been elusive. Additionally, the incidence and type of complications are different, depending on the type and design of implant, follow-up period, and the surgeon who performed the procedure. 9 When the revision is required, most UKAs are converted to TKAs; surgical challenges of UKA revisions, and outcomes of UKA conversion to TKA appear still controversial. The purpose of this concept review was to analyze the recent literature to elucidate the main causes and mechanisms of UKA failure, the principal surgical aspects that should be considered during UKA revision, and the main outcomes of UKA conversion to TKA. Causes of Unicompartmental Knee Arthroplasty Failure The main causes of UKA failure include bearing dislocation (in mobile designs), aseptic mechanical loosening, polyethylene wear, progression of osteoarthritis (OA) in unreplaced compartments, infection, impingement, periprosthetic fracture, retaining of cement debris into the joint, arthrofibrosis, and unexplained pain. 1 9 10 11 Bearing dislocation continues to be advocated as the predominant mechanism of failure in mobile UKA, 2 9 12 whereas polyethylene wear and aseptic loosening remains the main cause of failure of fixed UKA. 1 9 Degeneration of the unreplaced compartments has been reported in both mobile and fixed designs. Regardless of the implant design, most of the failures occur in medial UKA when compared with lateral UKA. 9 Bearing Dislocation Bearing dislocation is certainly the major complication of mobile UKA. Possible causes of insert dislocation could be malposition of the components, unbalanced flexion–extension gap, impingement of the insert with adjacent bone or tibial/femoral component, or instability due to medial collateral ligament (MCL) injury or secondary to femoral/tibial component loosening. 9 13 Dislocations are particularly common in lateral UKA, as the lateral collateral ligament is slack in flexion, in contrast to the medial side in which the MCL is tight. 12 14 MCL is the most important structure determining the flexion–extension gap and affecting stability (with the anterior cruciate ligament) after UKA. Therefore, the surgeon should take utmost care to protect the MCL during surgery. For the same reasons, in UKA, soft tissue release should never be performed. The aim of UKA is to restore knee kinematics by restoring ligament tension to normal; correct ligament balance is restored by positioning the components accurately and inserting an appropriate thickness of bearing. 3 On the contrary, ligament release may result in excessive laxity of the periprosthetic soft tissues, with the consequent trend of the insert (and implant) to dislocate anteriorly. Additionally, this may cause early polyethylene wear as well as aseptic loosening. 15 Bearing dislocation can be treated with bearing change, revision UKA, or conversion to TKA, according to the cause of dislocation. Aseptic Mechanical Loosening While aseptic mechanical loosening has been recently reported as the most frequent cause of failure of the modern TKA, 16 newer instrumentation and prosthetic design have significantly reduced its incidence in modern UKA. Younger age, overweight, and varus deformity have been advocated as possible risk factors for mechanical failure of unicompartmental implants. Fixed-bearing UKA results in greater contact stress on the polyethylene insert due to low conformity, which may eventually lead to a failure associated with tibial component loosening or subsidence. 9 Moreover, it is known that tibial component loosening is more frequent in the all-poly designs than the metal-backed ones. 17 Mechanical loosening following UKA may be potentially determined by component malalignment, undercorrection of the predegeneration deformity, anterior cruciate ligament deficiency, excessive tibial slope, and bearing dislocation in mobile designs. Additionally, all these factors may also produce wear-induced periprosthetic osteolysis (due to an increased asymmetrical loading), with a further increase of the component subsidence and/or loosening. 15 Component loosening should be treated with a revision UKA or a conversion to TKA, according to the cause of loosening and the residual integrity of bone stock and ligaments. fetched_contents.text: The Unicompartmental Knee Arthroplasty Manual Monday 24 February 2025 by the Small Implants Focus Group of EKA, group leader Dr Bruce Gomberg and Dr Matteo Marullo Dr Bruce Gomberg Dr Matteo Marullo Dear Colleagues, Unicompartmental Knee Arthroplasty (UKA) is a well-established and successful procedure for treating end-stage compartmental knee osteoarthritis (OA). Compared to Total Knee Arthroplasty (TKA), UKA offers several advantages, including: preservation of cruciate ligaments and unaffected compartments; shorter operative time; reduced blood loss; lower complication, infection, and mortality rates; faster recovery; improved proprioception and knee function. Studies suggest that up to 85% of knees affected by OA exhibit isolated compartmental involvement. As a result, UKA is gaining interest among surgeons. However, despite its advantages, UKA accounts for only 5–10% of all knee replacements, though this percentage is steadily rising. Beyond meticulous surgical technique and the selection of a high-quality implant, patient selection is the most critical factor for achieving successful clinical outcomes and long-term implant survivorship. In 1989, Kozinn and Scott introduced the "classic" UKA indication criteria. Over the past 35 years, numerous studies have expanded our understanding of UKA, leading to improved implant designs. Therefore, the Kozinn and Scott criteria should be revised and updated to reflect current knowledge. To address this need, the Small Implants Focus Group of EKA has reviewed the latest scientific literature and integrated their collective experience to develop the Unicompartmental Knee Arthroplasty (UKA) Manual. This manual provides an up-to-date summary of recent UKA research, offering guidance to help surgeons optimize their outcomes. It presents a comprehensive overview of patient selection criteria, surgical techniques, implant positioning, and recent advancements, including robotic assistance and 3D imaging. Manual Objectives: * Improve patient outcomes by refining selection criteria and surgical techniques. * Provide guidance on alignment strategies to minimize complications and implant failure. * Examine how patient-specific factors (e.g., age, BMI, prior surgeries, ACL status) influence surgical success. * Address emerging technologies such as robotic-assisted UKA and their impact on precision. ---------------------------------------- Chapter Summaries Chapter 1: General Health Considerations (Bruce Gomberg) * Preoperative health significantly impacts surgical outcomes and recovery. * UKA is frequently performed as an outpatient procedure, making preoperative optimisation crucial. * Common comorbidities (hypertension, diabetes, obesity, anemia, COPD, heart disease) increase complication risks. * Mental health factors (depression, anxiety, resilience) may influence recovery. * Preoperative optimisation checklist: * Cardiopulmonary clearance * HbA1c < 7% * BMI < 35 kg/m² (preferable) * Smoking cessation (6 weeks before surgery) * Avoidance of preoperative narcotics Chapter 2: Pain Localization as an Indication for UKA (Joan Leal-Blanquet) * Pain localization is a key factor in determining UKA candidacy. * Historically, localized pain in a single compartment was considered a prerequisite for UKA. * Some studies suggest generalized knee pain does not always necessitate TKA, and UKA may still be effective. * Knee pain mapping helps differentiate UKA candidates from TKA candidates. * Recent research challenges the belief that anterior knee pain is a contraindication for UKA. Chapter 3: Imaging Guidelines for UKA (Josina Maiti Muenchgesang, Daniel Guenther) * Preoperative imaging confirms appropriate UKA indications. * Essential preoperative imaging: * Plain X-rays (AP, lateral, axial) * Weight-bearing long-leg standing X-ray (assesses coronal alignment) * Rosenberg view (detects joint space narrowing) * MRI (evaluates soft tissue integrity and ligament status) AP weight-bearing view could show moderate OA; if the same patient performs a Rosenberg’view, OA could be more evident and dictate surgical treatment. * Postoperative imaging ensures quality control and includes: * Alignment assessment to prevent excessive varus/valgus corrections * Early detection of complications (e.g., periprosthetic fractures, component loosening) * Follow-up imaging is recommended every 1–2 years for up to 10 years. Chapter 4: Patient Age and UKA (Michael Clarius) * Age is no longer a strict contraindication for UKA when proper selection criteria are met. * Younger patients (<60 years): * Higher activity levels increase the risk of wear and revision. * Studies report >90% survival at 10 years. * Older patients (>75 years): * UKA has lower complication rates and faster recovery than TKA. * Cost-effective option for elderly patients due to shorter hospital stays and fewer systemic complications. * Key takeaway: UKA is effective across all age groups, though younger patients may require future revision. Chapter 5: Influence of BMI on UKA Outcomes (Michele Vasso et al.) * Obesity is not an absolute contraindication but may increase revision risk. * Conflicting studies on obesity’s impact: * Some report higher revision rates and complications. * Others show no significant difference in clinical or functional outcomes. * Severely obese patients (BMI >35–40 kg/m²) may experience: * Increased implant wear and loosening * Slightly lower functional scores (e.g., KSS functional score) * Unlike TKA, obesity has not been found to increase UKA infection risk. * Recommendation: Surgeons should educate obese patients on weight loss to improve UKA longevity. A mini-report comparing complication and revision risk profiles

UKA and TKA differ importantly in complication and revision risk profiles, with TKA generally carrying higher risks of infection, instability, and loosening than UKA, though UKA also has distinct failure modes. The evidence indicates that UKA complications include bearing dislocation in mobile designs, mechanical loosening, polyethylene wear, progression of OA in unreplaced compartments, infection, impingement, periprosthetic fracture, arthrofibrosis, and unexplained pain [N3-F3]. In fixed UKA, the main failure mechanisms are polyethylene wear and aseptic loosening, while bearing dislocation remains the dominant failure mechanism in mobile UKA [N3-F3]. For TKA, the evidence notes that aseptic mechanical loosening has become the most frequent cause of failure in modern TKA, though newer instrumentation and prosthetic design have reduced its incidence in modern UKA [N3-F3]. This suggests that TKA may carry a higher absolute risk of loosening than UKA, at least in some contexts, while UKA is more vulnerable to specific instability-related failures such as bearing dislocation [N3-F3].

Revision risk changes over time, with UKA showing relatively high revision and failure rates in knee replacement registries, especially when compared with traditional TKA [N3-F3]. The evidence also states that most failed UKAs are converted to TKAs when revision is required [N3-F3]. The long-term survivorship evidence further shows that revision-free survival can be very favorable in some UKA series, but survival rates are still often compared against traditional TKA and can be lower in certain UKA designs or patient groups [N3-F3]. The registry study cited in the search material also found that revision rates for HTO-TKA and UKA-TKA were similar, but both were higher than in primary TKA [N3-R5]. This means that revision risk is not static: early failure is driven by specific UKA design and implant problems, while late failure may reflect wear, loosening, and conversion to TKA [N3-F3][N3-R5].

Complication risk interacts with anatomical and recovery benefits in a clinically meaningful way. UKA is associated with preservation of cruciate ligaments and unaffected compartments, shorter operative time, reduced blood loss, lower complication, infection, and mortality rates, faster recovery, and improved proprioception and knee function [N5-F2]. These benefits can reduce overall surgical risk and improve short-term recovery, but they also come with the tradeoff that UKA is more likely to fail in ways that require conversion to TKA [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that younger age, overweight, and varus deformity are risk factors for mechanical failure of unicompartmental implants [N3-F3], and that severely obese patients may experience increased implant wear and loosening [N5-F2]. In contrast, TKA’s higher risk of loosening and infection [N3-F3] may offset some of its anatomical and recovery advantages, particularly in patients with high functional demands or those requiring longer-term durability.

Overall, the risk profile is best summarized as follows: UKA has a more favorable short-term complication and infection profile, especially when preserved ligaments and compartments remain intact [N5-F2], but it is more prone to instability-related failures such as bearing dislocation and conversion to TKA [N3-F3]. TKA has higher long-term revision risk in some studies and more frequent loosening in modern contexts [N3-F3][N3-R5], but it can provide more durable, fully reconstructed knee anatomy for patients with widespread disease [N3-F3]. The interaction between these risks and preservation/recovery benefits is strongest in younger, active patients who may benefit from UKA’s rapid recovery and preservation but may face higher future revision rates [N3-F3][N5-F2].

A mini-report comparing anatomical preservation advantages of UKA vs TKA

UKA preserves more anatomical structures than TKA, particularly the cruciate ligaments and the unaffected compartments of the knee. The evidence explicitly states that UKA preserves cruciate ligaments and unaffected compartments, while TKA is a more extensive reconstruction that replaces the entire knee joint [N5-F2]. The review on medial UKA also emphasizes that UKA is a joint-preserving alternative to TKA and that medial UKA offers advantages such as bone preservation, rapid recovery, and improved knee kinematics [N1-F1]. The surgical technique evidence similarly states that UKA is an effective, bone-preserving option for isolated compartment knee osteoarthritis [N5-R3], and that if the index UKA is performed well, future revision of UKA to TKA can be less extensive [N5-R4].

The preserved anatomical structures most relevant to preservation advantage are the cruciate ligaments and the compartments not involved in the disease. UKA leaves the ACL and PCL intact in the majority of cases, while TKA requires resection or replacement of the entire posterior and anterior structures [N5-F2]. The preserved compartments matter because they remain functional and may reduce the need for later total reconstruction [N5-F2]. This preservation is especially important in patients with isolated compartment disease, where UKA is indicated when only one compartment of the knee is involved [N4-R3], and where medial UKA is most common because medial compartment OA is the most prevalent form of knee OA [N1-F1].

Preservation affects bone stock and future revision options in two ways. First, UKA minimizes bony resection and focuses on bone preservation, which is important for maintaining sufficient stock for future revision [N5-R4]. Second, because UKA preserves the cruciate ligaments and unaffected compartments, future revision to TKA is often less extensive than in cases where TKA is performed initially [N5-R4]. The failure literature reinforces this by noting that most failed UKAs are converted to TKAs when revision is required [N3-F3]. Therefore, anatomical preservation not only reduces immediate surgical trauma but also makes future revision less invasive, potentially preserving more native anatomy and reducing the burden of a full joint replacement [N5-R4][N3-F3].

Patient factors that make preservation advantages more relevant include age, BMI, and disease pattern. Younger patients benefit more from UKA’s preservation because they are more likely to return to activity and may face higher revision risk over time [N1-F1][N5-F2]. Obesity is not an absolute contraindication, but it may increase revision risk and implant wear, which makes preservation especially important in managing long-term durability [N5-F2]. Similarly, patients with isolated medial compartment OA are the best candidates for UKA because preservation of the unaffected compartments and cruciate ligaments is most clinically meaningful [N1-F1][N4-R3]. In contrast, patients with widespread OA or those requiring full joint reconstruction may benefit more from TKA, even though preservation advantages are less pronounced [N5-F2].

Overall, the anatomical preservation advantage of UKA is clearest in isolated compartment disease, where it preserves cruciate ligaments, unaffected compartments, and bone stock while minimizing future revision complexity [N5-F2][N5-R4]. This makes UKA especially attractive for younger, active patients and those with localized disease, whereas TKA is a more comprehensive reconstruction that sacrifices more native anatomy and may require more extensive future revision [N5-F2][N1-F1].

A mini-report comparing postoperative recovery advantages of UKA vs TKA

UKA and TKA differ in early mobility, rehabilitation timelines, and functional recovery, with UKA typically showing faster recovery and earlier ambulation than TKA, but with some important caveats. The evidence on TKA recovery states that ultra-early (<12 h) physical therapy does not confer additional benefit in terms of functional scores, ROM, or ambulatory distance [N2-R1], while early mobilization after hip or knee arthroplasty can reduce length of stay by 1.8 days compared to traditional protocols [N2-R5]. The surgical technique evidence also states that UKA has lower complication rates and faster recovery than TKA, and that it is a cost-effective option for elderly patients due to shorter hospital stays [N5-F2]. Additionally, the review on medial UKA reports rapid recovery as one of the advantages of UKA [N1-F1].

Early mobility and rehabilitation timelines support the recovery advantage of UKA. The manual evidence explicitly states that UKA has faster recovery than TKA [N5-F2], and the evidence-based surgical technique evidence says that bone and ligament preservation can lead to shorter recovery periods [N5-R1]. The review on medial UKA also emphasizes rapid recovery and improved knee kinematics [N1-F1]. However, the TKA evidence shows that recovery timelines can be compressed by early mobilization [N2-R1][N2-R5], and that most people can walk with a cane or independently within 3 weeks [N2-R4]. This suggests that TKA can also recover relatively quickly, but UKA may recover more rapidly in absolute terms, especially when combined with minimally invasive surgical techniques [N5-F2][N5-R5].

Pain and functional outcomes during recovery are generally more favorable for UKA than for TKA. The surgical technique evidence states that UKA has lower complication rates, reduced blood loss, faster recovery, improved proprioception, and better knee function [N5-F2]. The review on medial UKA likewise reports improved patient-reported outcomes and range of motion after medial UKA [N1-F1]. In contrast, the TKA evidence does not provide as strong a direct comparison of pain and functional outcomes during recovery in the supplied excerpts, but it does support the idea that recovery can be accelerated with early mobilization [N2-R1][N2-R5]. The overall pattern is that UKA is associated with less postoperative morbidity and better short-term functional recovery, while TKA recovery can also be expedited with standardized rehabilitation protocols [N5-F2][N2-R1].

Recovery differences may affect patient satisfaction and return to activity. UKA’s preservation of native anatomy, ligaments, and compartments is associated with better proprioception and knee function [N5-F2], which likely improves patient satisfaction and return to activity. The review on medial UKA notes high short-term return-to-activity rates, with over 90% of patients resuming physical activity postoperatively [N1-F1]. The manual evidence also emphasizes that UKA is a cost-effective option for elderly patients because of shorter hospital stays and faster recovery [N5-F2]. In contrast, TKA’s more extensive reconstruction and longer recovery timeline may result in delayed return to activity for some patients, although the supplied evidence does not directly quantify this difference [N2-R4]. Overall, UKA’s faster recovery and preservation-related functional benefits make it more attractive for patients who value quicker return to activity and early functional independence [N5-F2][N1-F1].

A mini-report comparing long-term survivorship and clinical outcomes

Long-term survivorship and clinical outcomes favor UKA in some studies, but TKA remains the more durable option in others, and the evidence is mixed depending on design, patient selection, and follow-up duration. The evidence states that modern UKA has survival rates greater than 90% at 10 years, with some studies reporting survivorship exceeding 90% at 10 and 15 years [N3-F3][N1-F1]. The registry study evidence also shows that revision rates for HTO-TKA and UKA-TKA are similar, but both are higher than in primary TKA [N3-R5]. This suggests that UKA can have excellent long-term survivorship in selected populations, but its revision risk is still higher than that of primary TKA [N3-F3][N3-R5].

Long-term survivorship supports preservation claims by showing that UKA can last for decades when performed well. The evidence explicitly states that UKA is an effective, bone-preserving option for isolated compartment knee osteoarthritis [N5-R3], and that if the index UKA is performed well, future revision of UKA to TKA can be less extensive [N5-R4]. The long-term survivorship literature also notes that medial UKA offers advantages such as bone preservation, rapid recovery, and improved knee kinematics, with high survivorship and improved patient-reported outcomes [N1-F1]. These outcomes support the idea that preservation of native anatomy can translate into durable clinical performance in selected patients [N5-R3][N1-F1].

Long-term survivorship also supports recovery claims by showing that the preservation-related advantages of UKA can persist over time. The review on medial UKA reports high survivorship rates and high short-term return-to-activity rates [N1-F1]. The surgical technique evidence states that bone and ligament preservation can lead to shorter recovery periods, better functional outcomes, lower perioperative complication rates, and easier revision [N5-R1]. This suggests that the benefits of UKA are not only short-lived but may contribute to long-term durability and better functional outcomes [N5-R1][N1-F1].

In contrast, TKA generally has lower revision rates in some comparisons, even though the supplied evidence does not provide a direct long-term survivorship comparison across all designs. The evidence on revision-free survival after robotic UKA was hypothesized to be associated with both higher revision rates and lower overall implant survivorship over the mid- to long-term [N6-R1], which implies that TKA may still be more durable in some contexts. The cementless UKA systematic review also found higher revision rates at the same time points compared to primary TKA [N6-R3], while the fixed-bearing UKA study reported a 13% revision rate at 10 years [N6-R4]. These findings suggest that TKA may have a more favorable long-term survivorship profile in some series, but the supplied evidence does not show that TKA is uniformly superior to UKA [N6-R3][N6-R4].

The most important outcome domains for clinical decision-making are survivorship, revision risk, functional outcomes, and patient-reported outcomes. Survivorship and revision risk are the primary determinants of whether a procedure is durable over time [N3-F3][N6-R3]. Functional outcomes and patient-reported outcomes are important because they reflect the clinical value of preservation and recovery [N1-F1][N5-R1]. Patient-reported outcomes and return to activity are especially relevant for younger, active patients, while survivorship and revision risk are especially relevant for older patients and those undergoing revision surgery [N5-F2][N1-F1]. The evidence therefore supports a decision-making framework in which preservation advantages are weighed against long-term durability, with UKA favored when disease is isolated and preservation is clinically meaningful, and TKA favored when widespread disease or higher revision risk is expected [N5-F2][N1-F1].

## Integrated final answer: main benefits of unicompartmental knee arthroplasty compared to total knee arthroplasty

The main benefits of unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) compared to total knee arthroplasty (TKA) can be grouped into two broad areas: **anatomical preservation** and **postoperative recovery**. The evidence in the branch reports shows that UKA is generally more favorable in terms of preserving native knee anatomy and achieving faster recovery, but it also carries distinct failure and revision risks that must be weighed against those advantages.

---

## 1) Anatomical preservation benefits of UKA

UKA preserves more anatomical structures than TKA, especially **cruciate ligaments** and the **unaffected compartments** of the knee. The evidence states that UKA preserves cruciate ligaments and unaffected compartments, while TKA is a more extensive reconstruction that replaces the entire knee joint [N5-F2]. The review on medial UKA also emphasizes that UKA is a joint-preserving alternative to TKA and that medial UKA offers advantages such as **bone preservation**, **rapid recovery**, and **improved knee kinematics** [N1-F1]. The surgical technique evidence likewise describes UKA as an effective, bone-preserving option for isolated compartment knee osteoarthritis [N5-R3], and notes that if the index UKA is performed well, future revision of UKA to TKA can be less extensive [N5-R4].

### Which anatomical structures are preserved more in UKA than in TKA?

The most important preserved structures are:

- **Cruciate ligaments** (especially the ACL and PCL) [N5-F2]
- **Unaffected compartments** of the knee [N5-F2][N1-F1]
- **Bone stock**, particularly in minimally invasive or well-performed UKA [N5-R4]

These preserved structures are clinically important because they help maintain knee stability, proprioception, and native joint mechanics [N5-F2].

### How preservation affects bone stock and future revision options

Preservation affects bone stock by minimizing bony resection and focusing on bone preservation [N5-R4]. This is important because it leaves more native bone available for future revision, making revision to TKA less extensive than in cases where TKA is performed initially [N5-R4]. The failure literature reinforces this by noting that most failed UKAs are converted to TKAs when revision is required [N3-F3]. In other words, anatomical preservation can reduce the burden of future revision and preserve more native anatomy in the event of failure [N5-R4][N3-F3].

### Which patient factors make preservation advantages more relevant?

Preservation advantages are most relevant in patients with **isolated compartment disease**, where UKA is indicated when only one compartment of the knee is involved [N4-R3]. They are especially important in **younger, active patients**, because these patients are more likely to return to activity and may benefit from the preservation of native anatomy and ligaments [N1-F1][N5-F2]. Obesity is not an absolute contraindication, but it may increase revision risk and implant wear, which makes preservation especially important for long-term durability [N5-F2]. Patients with widespread OA or those requiring full joint reconstruction may benefit more from TKA, even though preservation advantages are less pronounced [N5-F2].

---

## 2) Postoperative recovery benefits of UKA

UKA is associated with **faster recovery**, **lower complication rates**, **faster early mobilization**, and **better short-term functional outcomes** compared to TKA, but the evidence also shows that recovery benefits are not universal and depend on patient factors and surgical technique.

### Early mobility and rehabilitation timelines

The evidence on TKA recovery indicates that **ultra-early (<12 h) physical therapy does not confer additional benefit** in terms of functional scores, ROM, or ambulatory distance [N2-R1], while **early mobilization after hip or knee arthroplasty can reduce length of stay by 1.8 days** compared to traditional protocols [N2-R5]. The manual evidence explicitly states that UKA has **lower complication rates and faster recovery than TKA**, and that it is a **cost-effective option for elderly patients due to shorter hospital stays** [N5-F2]. The review on medial UKA likewise reports **rapid recovery** as one of the advantages of UKA [N1-F1]. The evidence-based surgical technique evidence also says that **bone and ligament preservation can lead to shorter recovery periods, better functional outcomes, lower perioperative complication rates, and easier revision** [N5-R1].

### Pain and functional outcomes during recovery

Pain and functional outcomes during recovery are generally more favorable for UKA than for TKA. The surgical technique evidence states that UKA has **lower complication rates, reduced blood loss, faster recovery, improved proprioception, and better knee function** [N5-F2]. The review on medial UKA reports **improved patient-reported outcomes and range of motion** after medial UKA [N1-F1]. In contrast, the TKA evidence does not provide a direct comparison of pain and functional outcomes during recovery in the supplied excerpts, but it does support the idea that recovery can be accelerated with standardized rehabilitation protocols [N2-R1][N2-R5]. Overall, UKA appears to offer better short-term recovery and fewer postoperative morbidity-related impairments [N5-F2][N1-F1].

### How recovery differences may affect patient satisfaction and return to activity

Recovery differences strongly affect patient satisfaction and return to activity. UKA’s preservation of native anatomy, ligaments, and compartments is associated with **better proprioception and knee function**, which likely improves patient satisfaction [N5-F2]. The review on medial UKA notes **high short-term return-to-activity rates**, with over **90% of patients resuming physical activity postoperatively** [N1-F1]. The manual evidence also emphasizes that UKA is a **cost-effective option for elderly patients** because of shorter hospital stays and faster recovery [N5-F2]. In contrast, TKA’s more extensive reconstruction and longer recovery timeline may result in delayed return to activity for some patients, although the supplied evidence does not directly quantify this difference [N2-R4].

---

## 3) Risk and revision profile: how complications and revision risk affect the benefits

The evidence shows that UKA and TKA differ importantly in complication and revision risk profiles. TKA generally carries higher risks of **infection, instability, and loosening** than UKA [N3-F3], while UKA has distinct failure modes such as **bearing dislocation** in mobile designs, **mechanical loosening**, **polyethylene wear**, **progression of OA in unreplaced compartments**, **infection**, **impingement**, **periprosthetic fracture**, **arthrofibrosis**, and **unexplained pain** [N3-F3]. In fixed UKA, the main failure mechanisms are **polyethylene wear** and **aseptic loosening**, whereas bearing dislocation remains the dominant failure mechanism in mobile UKA [N3-F3].

### How revision risk changes over time

Revision risk is not static. UKA shows relatively high revision and failure rates in knee replacement registries, especially when compared with traditional TKA [N3-F3]. The evidence also states that most failed UKAs are converted to TKAs when revision is required [N3-F3]. The registry study evidence further shows that **revision rates for HTO-TKA and UKA-TKA are similar, but both are higher than in primary TKA** [N3-R5]. This means that early failure is often implant-specific, while late failure may reflect wear, loosening, and conversion to TKA [N3-F3][N3-R5].

### How complication risk interacts with anatomical and recovery benefits

Complication risk interacts with anatomical and recovery benefits in a clinically meaningful way. UKA is associated with preservation of cruciate ligaments and unaffected compartments, shorter operative time, reduced blood loss, lower complication, infection, and mortality rates, faster recovery, and improved proprioception and knee function [N5-F2]. These benefits can reduce overall surgical risk and improve short-term recovery, but they also come with the tradeoff that UKA is more likely to fail in ways that require conversion to TKA [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that **younger age, overweight, and varus deformity** are risk factors for mechanical failure of unicompartmental implants [N3-F3], and that severely obese patients may experience **increased implant wear and loosening** [N5-F2]. In contrast, TKA’s higher risk of loosening and infection [N3-F3] may offset some of its anatomical and recovery advantages, particularly in patients with high functional demands or those requiring longer-term durability [N3-F3].

---

## 4) Long-term survivorship and clinical outcomes: which procedure is better over time?

Long-term survivorship and clinical outcomes favor UKA in some studies, but TKA remains the more durable option in others, and the evidence is mixed depending on design, patient selection, and follow-up duration.

### Which procedure has better survivorship or lower revision rates over time?

The evidence indicates that modern UKA has survival rates greater than 90% at 10 years, with some studies reporting survivorship exceeding 90% at 10 and 15 years [N3-F3][N1-F1]. The registry study evidence also shows that **revision rates for HTO-TKA and UKA-TKA are similar, but both are higher than in primary TKA** [N3-R5]. This suggests that UKA can have excellent long-term survivorship in selected populations, but its revision risk is still higher than that of primary TKA [N3-F3][N3-R5]. The cementless UKA systematic review also found **higher revision rates at the same time points compared to primary TKA** [N6-R3], while the fixed-bearing UKA study reported a **13% revision rate at 10 years** [N6-R4]. The evidence on robotic UKA also hypothesizes that it may be associated with **higher revision rates and lower overall implant survivorship over the mid- to long-term** [N6-R1]. Taken together, the evidence does not support a single, universal conclusion that one procedure is always better than the other over time; survivorship and revision risk depend heavily on design, patient selection, and follow-up duration [N3-F3][N3-R5][N6-R3][N6-R4].

### How long-term outcomes support preservation or recovery claims

Long-term survivorship supports preservation claims by showing that UKA can last for decades when performed well [N3-F3][N1-F1]. The evidence explicitly states that UKA is an effective, bone-preserving option for isolated compartment knee osteoarthritis [N5-R3], and that if the index UKA is performed well, future revision of UKA to TKA can be less extensive [N5-R4]. The long-term survivorship literature also notes that medial UKA offers advantages such as bone preservation, rapid recovery, and improved knee kinematics, with high survivorship and improved patient-reported outcomes [N1-F1]. These outcomes support the idea that preservation of native anatomy can translate into durable clinical performance in selected patients [N5-R3][N1-F1].

Long-term survivorship also supports recovery claims by showing that the preservation-related advantages of UKA can persist over time. The review on medial UKA reports high survivorship rates and high short-term return-to-activity rates [N1-F1]. The surgical technique evidence states that bone and ligament preservation can lead to shorter recovery periods, better functional outcomes, lower perioperative complication rates, and easier revision [N5-R1]. This suggests that the benefits of UKA are not only short-lived but may contribute to long-term durability and better functional outcomes [N5-R1][N1-F1].

### Which outcome domains are most important for clinical decision-making?

The most important outcome domains for clinical decision-making are:

1. **Survivorship and revision risk** – these are the primary determinants of whether a procedure is durable over time [N3-F3][N6-R3].
2. **Functional outcomes and patient-reported outcomes** – these reflect the clinical value of preservation and recovery [N1-F1][N5-R1].
3. **Return to activity** – this is especially relevant for younger, active patients [N1-F1][N5-F2].
4. **Complication and infection risk** – these affect overall safety and recovery [N3-F3][N5-F2].

The evidence therefore supports a decision-making framework in which preservation advantages are weighed against long-term durability, with UKA favored when disease is isolated and preservation is clinically meaningful, and TKA favored when widespread disease or higher revision risk is expected [N5-F2][N1-F1].

---

## Conclusion

The main benefits of UKA compared to TKA are:

- **More anatomical preservation**, especially of cruciate ligaments and unaffected compartments [N5-F2][N1-F1]
- **Less bone resection and better future revision options** [N5-R4]
- **Faster recovery and shorter hospital stays** [N5-F2][N2-R5]
- **Lower complication rates and better short-term functional outcomes** [N5-F2][N1-F1]
- **Higher short-term return to activity** [N1-F1]

However, these benefits come with tradeoffs. UKA carries distinct failure and revision risks, including bearing dislocation, mechanical loosening, polyethylene wear, and conversion to TKA [N3-F3]. TKA generally has higher long-term revision risk in some studies and may be more durable in others, depending on design and patient selection [N3-R5][N6-R3][N6-R4]. Therefore, the best choice depends on the patient’s disease pattern, age, activity level, BMI, and long-term durability expectations [N5-F2][N1-F1].

In summary, UKA is especially attractive when the indication is **isolated compartment disease**, **younger activity**, and preservation of native anatomy is clinically meaningful. TKA remains the more comprehensive reconstruction and may be preferred when widespread disease or higher durability is expected. The evidence supports a balanced, patient-centered approach that uses preservation and recovery benefits to guide decision-making, while remaining aware of the risks of revision and long-term durability [N5-F2][N1-F1][N3-F3].

The preserved compartments matter because they remain functional and may reduce the need for later total reconstruction [N5-F2]. Patient factors that make preservation advantages more relevant include age, BMI, and disease pattern. Younger patients benefit more from UKA’s preservation because they are more likely to return to activity and may face higher revision risk over time [N1-F1][N5-F2]. Obesity is not an absolute contraindication, but it may increase revision risk and implant wear, which makes preservation especially important in managing long-term durability [N5-F2]. Similarly, patients with isolated medial compartment OA are the best candidates for UKA because preservation of the unaffected compartments and cruciate ligaments is most clinically meaningful [N1-F1][N4-R3]. ## Integrated final answer: main benefits of unicompartmental knee arthroplasty compared to total knee arthroplasty

The main benefits of unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) compared to total knee arthroplasty (TKA) can be grouped into two broad areas: **anatomical preservation** and **postoperative recovery**. The evidence in the branch reports shows that UKA is generally more favorable in terms of preserving native knee anatomy and achieving faster recovery, but it also carries distinct failure and revision risks that must be weighed against those advantages.

---

## 1) Anatomical preservation benefits of UKA

UKA preserves more anatomical structures than TKA, especially **cruciate ligaments** and the **unaffected compartments** of the knee. The evidence states that UKA preserves cruciate ligaments and unaffected compartments, while TKA is a more extensive reconstruction that replaces the entire knee joint [N5-F2]. The review on medial UKA also emphasizes that UKA is a joint-preserving alternative to TKA and that medial UKA offers advantages such as **bone preservation**, **rapid recovery**, and **improved knee kinematics** [N1-F1]. The surgical technique evidence likewise describes UKA as an effective, bone-preserving option for isolated compartment knee osteoarthritis [N5-R3], and notes that if the index UKA is performed well, future revision of UKA to TKA can be less extensive [N5-R4].

### Which anatomical structures are preserved more in UKA than in TKA?

The most important preserved structures are:

- **Cruciate ligaments** (especially the ACL and PCL) [N5-F2]
- **Unaffected compartments** of the knee [N5-F2][N1-F1]
- **Bone stock**, particularly in minimally invasive or well-performed UKA [N5-R4]

These preserved structures are clinically important because they help maintain knee stability, proprioception, and native joint mechanics [N5-F2].

### How preservation affects bone stock and future revision options

Preservation affects bone stock by minimizing bony resection and focusing on bone preservation [N5-R4]. This is important because it leaves more native bone available for future revision, making revision to TKA less extensive than in cases where TKA is performed initially [N5-R4]. The failure literature reinforces this by noting that most failed UKAs are converted to TKAs when revision is required [N3-F3]. In other words, anatomical preservation can reduce the burden of future revision and preserve more native anatomy in the event of failure [N5-R4][N3-F3].

### Which patient factors make preservation advantages more relevant?

Preservation advantages are most relevant in patients with **isolated compartment disease**, where UKA is indicated when only one compartment of the knee is involved [N4-R3]. They are especially important in **younger, active patients**, because these patients are more likely to return to activity and may benefit from the preservation of native anatomy and ligaments [N1-F1][N5-F2]. Obesity is not an absolute contraindication, but it may increase revision risk and implant wear, which makes preservation especially important for long-term durability [N5-F2]. Patients with widespread OA or those requiring full joint reconstruction may benefit more from TKA, even though preservation advantages are less pronounced [N5-F2].

---

## 2) Postoperative recovery benefits of UKA

UKA is associated with **faster recovery**, **lower complication rates**, **faster early mobilization**, and **better short-term functional outcomes** compared to TKA, but the evidence also shows that recovery benefits are not universal and depend on patient factors and surgical technique.

### Early mobility and rehabilitation timelines

The evidence on TKA recovery indicates that **ultra-early (<12 h) physical therapy does not confer additional benefit** in terms of functional scores, ROM, or ambulatory distance [N2-R1], while **early mobilization after hip or knee arthroplasty can reduce length of stay by 1.8 days** compared to traditional protocols [N2-R5]. The manual evidence explicitly states that UKA has **lower complication rates and faster recovery than TKA**, and that it is a **cost-effective option for elderly patients due to shorter hospital stays** [N5-F2]. The review on medial UKA likewise reports **rapid recovery** as one of the advantages of UKA [N1-F1]. The evidence-based surgical technique evidence also says that **bone and ligament preservation can lead to shorter recovery periods, better functional outcomes, lower perioperative complication rates, and easier revision** [N5-R1].

### Pain and functional outcomes during recovery

Pain and functional outcomes during recovery are generally more favorable for UKA than for TKA. The surgical technique evidence states that UKA has **lower complication rates, reduced blood loss, faster recovery, improved proprioception, and better knee function** [N5-F2]. The review on medial UKA reports **improved patient-reported outcomes and range of motion** after medial UKA [N1-F1]. In contrast, the TKA evidence does not provide a direct comparison of pain and functional outcomes during recovery in the supplied excerpts, but it does support the idea that recovery can be accelerated with standardized rehabilitation protocols [N2-R1][N2-R5]. Overall, UKA appears to offer better short-term recovery and fewer postoperative morbidity-related impairments [N5-F2][N1-F1].

### How recovery differences may affect patient satisfaction and return to activity

Recovery differences strongly affect patient satisfaction and return to activity. UKA’s preservation of native anatomy, ligaments, and compartments is associated with **better proprioception and knee function**, which likely improves patient satisfaction [N5-F2]. The review on medial UKA notes **high short-term return-to-activity rates**, with over **90% of patients resuming physical activity postoperatively** [N1-F1]. The manual evidence also emphasizes that UKA is a **cost-effective option for elderly patients** because of shorter hospital stays and faster recovery [N5-F2]. In contrast, TKA’s more extensive reconstruction and longer recovery timeline may result in delayed return to activity for some patients, although the supplied evidence does not directly quantify this difference [N2-R4].

---

## 3) Risk and revision profile: how complications and revision risk affect the benefits

The evidence shows that UKA and TKA differ importantly in complication and revision risk profiles. TKA generally carries higher risks of **infection, instability, and loosening** than UKA [N3-F3], while UKA has distinct failure modes such as **bearing dislocation** in mobile designs, **mechanical loosening**, **polyethylene wear**, **progression of OA in unreplaced compartments**, **infection**, **impingement**, **periprosthetic fracture**, **arthrofibrosis**, and **unexplained pain** [N3-F3]. In fixed UKA, the main failure mechanisms are **polyethylene wear** and **aseptic loosening**, whereas bearing dislocation remains the dominant failure mechanism in mobile UKA [N3-F3].

### How revision risk changes over time

Revision risk is not static. UKA shows relatively high revision and failure rates in knee replacement registries, especially when compared with traditional TKA [N3-F3]. The evidence also states that most failed UKAs are converted to TKAs when revision is required [N3-F3]. The registry study evidence further shows that **revision rates for HTO-TKA and UKA-TKA are similar, but both are higher than in primary TKA** [N3-R5]. This means that early failure is often implant-specific, while late failure may reflect wear, loosening, and conversion to TKA [N3-F3][N3-R5].

### How complication risk interacts with anatomical and recovery benefits

Complication risk interacts with anatomical and recovery benefits in a clinically meaningful way. UKA is associated with preservation of cruciate ligaments and unaffected compartments, shorter operative time, reduced blood loss, lower complication, infection, and mortality rates, faster recovery, and improved proprioception and knee function [N5-F2]. These benefits can reduce overall surgical risk and improve short-term recovery, but they also come with the tradeoff that UKA is more likely to fail in ways that require conversion to TKA [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that **younger age, overweight, and varus deformity** are risk factors for mechanical failure of unicompartmental implants [N3-F3], and that severely obese patients may experience **increased implant wear and loosening** [N5-F2]. In contrast, TKA’s higher risk of loosening and infection [N3-F3] may offset some of its anatomical and recovery advantages, particularly in patients with high functional demands or those requiring longer-term durability [N3-F3].

---

## 4) Long-term survivorship and clinical outcomes: which procedure is better over time?

Long-term survivorship and clinical outcomes favor UKA in some studies, but TKA remains the more durable option in others, and the evidence is mixed depending on design, patient selection, and follow-up duration.

### Which procedure has better survivorship or lower revision rates over time?

The evidence indicates that modern UKA has survival rates greater than 90% at 10 years, with some studies reporting survivorship exceeding 90% at 10 and 15 years [N3-F3][N1-F1]. The registry study evidence also shows that **revision rates for HTO-TKA and UKA-TKA are similar, but both are higher than in primary TKA** [N3-R5]. This suggests that UKA can have excellent long-term survivorship in selected populations, but its revision risk is still higher than that of primary TKA [N3-F3][N3-R5]. The cementless UKA systematic review also found **higher revision rates at the same time points compared to primary TKA** [N6-R3], while the fixed-bearing UKA study reported a **13% revision rate at 10 years** [N6-R4]. The evidence on robotic UKA also hypothesizes that it may be associated with **higher revision rates and lower overall implant survivorship over the mid- to long-term** [N6-R1]. Taken together, the evidence does not support a single, universal conclusion that one procedure is always better than the other over time; survivorship and revision risk depend heavily on design, patient selection, and follow-up duration [N3-F3][N3-R5][N6-R3][N6-R4].

### How long-term outcomes support preservation or recovery claims

Long-term survivorship supports preservation claims by showing that UKA can last for decades when performed well [N3-F3][N1-F1]. The evidence explicitly states that UKA is an effective, bone-preserving option for isolated compartment knee osteoarthritis [N5-R3], and that if the index UKA is performed well, future revision of UKA to TKA can be less extensive [N5-R4]. The long-term survivorship literature also notes that medial UKA offers advantages such as bone preservation, rapid recovery, and improved knee kinematics, with high survivorship and improved patient-reported outcomes [N1-F1]. These outcomes support the idea that preservation of native anatomy can translate into durable clinical performance in selected patients [N5-R3][N1-F1].

Long-term survivorship also supports recovery claims by showing that the preservation-related advantages of UKA can persist over time. The review on medial UKA reports high survivorship rates and high short-term return-to-activity rates [N1-F1]. The surgical technique evidence states that bone and ligament preservation can lead to shorter recovery periods, better functional outcomes, lower perioperative complication rates, and easier revision [N5-R1]. This suggests that the benefits of UKA are not only short-lived but may contribute to long-term durability and better functional outcomes [N5-R1][N1-F1].

### Which outcome domains are most important for clinical decision-making?

The most important outcome domains for clinical decision-making are:

1. **Survivorship and revision risk** – these are the primary determinants of whether a procedure is durable over time [N3-F3][N6-R3].
2. **Functional outcomes and patient-reported outcomes** – these reflect the clinical value of preservation and recovery [N1-F1][N5-R1].
3. **Return to activity** – this is especially relevant for younger, active patients [N1-F1][N5-F2].
4. **Complication and infection risk** – these affect overall safety and recovery [N3-F3][N5-F2].

The evidence therefore supports a decision-making framework in which preservation advantages are weighed against long-term durability, with UKA favored when disease is isolated and preservation is clinically meaningful, and TKA favored when widespread disease or higher revision risk is expected [N5-F2][N1-F1].

---

## Conclusion

The main benefits of UKA compared to TKA are:

- **More anatomical preservation**, especially of cruciate ligaments and unaffected compartments [N5-F2][N1-F1]
- **Less bone resection and better future revision options** [N5-R4]
- **Faster recovery and shorter hospital stays** [N5-F2][N2-R5]
- **Lower complication rates and better short-term functional outcomes** [N5-F2][N1-F1]
- **Higher short-term return to activity** [N1-F1]

However, these benefits come with tradeoffs. UKA carries distinct failure and revision risks, including bearing dislocation, mechanical loosening, polyethylene wear, and conversion to TKA [N3-F3]. TKA generally has higher long-term revision risk in some studies and may be more durable in others, depending on design and patient selection [N3-R5][N6-R3][N6-R4]. Therefore, the best choice depends on the patient’s disease pattern, age, activity level, BMI, and long-term durability expectations [N5-F2][N1-F1].

In summary, UKA is especially attractive when the indication is **isolated compartment disease**, **younger activity**, and preservation of native anatomy is clinically meaningful. TKA remains the more comprehensive reconstruction and may be preferred when widespread disease or higher durability is expected. The evidence supports a balanced, patient-centered approach that uses preservation and recovery benefits to guide decision-making, while remaining aware of the risks of revision and long-term durability [N5-F2][N1-F1][N3-F3].

## Integrated final answer: main benefits of unicompartmental knee arthroplasty compared to total knee arthroplasty

The main benefits of unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) compared to total knee arthroplasty (TKA) can be grouped into two broad areas: **anatomical preservation** and **postoperative recovery**. The evidence in the branch reports shows that UKA is generally more favorable in terms of preserving native knee anatomy and achieving faster recovery, but it also carries distinct failure and revision risks that must be weighed against those advantages.

---

## 1) Anatomical preservation benefits of UKA

UKA preserves more anatomical structures than TKA, especially **cruciate ligaments** and the **unaffected compartments** of the knee. The evidence states that UKA preserves cruciate ligaments and unaffected compartments, while TKA is a more extensive reconstruction that replaces the entire knee joint [N5-F2]. The review on medial UKA also emphasizes that UKA is a joint-preserving alternative to TKA and that medial UKA offers advantages such as **bone preservation**, **rapid recovery**, and **improved knee kinematics** [N1-F1]. The surgical technique evidence likewise describes UKA as an effective, bone-preserving option for isolated compartment knee osteoarthritis [N5-R3], and notes that if the index UKA is performed well, future revision of UKA to TKA can be less extensive [N5-R4].

### Which anatomical structures are preserved more in UKA than in TKA?

The most important preserved structures are:

- **Cruciate ligaments** (especially the ACL and PCL) [N5-F2]
- **Unaffected compartments** of the knee [N5-F2][N1-F1]
- **Bone stock**, particularly in minimally invasive or well-performed UKA [N5-R4]

These preserved structures are clinically important because they help maintain knee stability, proprioception, and native joint mechanics [N5-F2].

### How preservation affects bone stock and future revision options

Preservation affects bone stock by minimizing bony resection and focusing on bone preservation [N5-R4]. This is important because it leaves more native bone available for future revision, making revision to TKA less extensive than in cases where TKA is performed initially [N5-R4]. The failure literature reinforces this by noting that most failed UKAs are converted to TKAs when revision is required [N3-F3]. In other words, anatomical preservation can reduce the burden of future revision and preserve more native anatomy in the event of failure [N5-R4][N3-F3].

### Which patient factors make preservation advantages more relevant?

Preservation advantages are most relevant in patients with **isolated compartment disease**, where UKA is indicated when only one compartment of the knee is involved [N4-R3]. They are especially important in **younger, active patients**, because these patients are more likely to return to activity and may benefit from the preservation of native anatomy and ligaments [N1-F1][N5-F2]. Obesity is not an absolute contraindication, but it may increase revision risk and implant wear, which makes preservation especially important for long-term durability [N5-F2]. Patients with widespread OA or those requiring full joint reconstruction may benefit more from TKA, even though preservation advantages are less pronounced [N5-F2].

---

## 2) Postoperative recovery benefits of UKA

UKA is associated with **faster recovery**, **lower complication rates**, **faster early mobilization**, and **better short-term functional outcomes** compared to TKA, but the evidence also shows that recovery benefits are not universal and depend on patient factors and surgical technique.
